items.headline: Gold/silver close out the week lower into the weekend close -- GLD $380.14 (-0.68%), SLV $54.74 (-0.51%), silver futures $59.98 (-1.23%), gold futures $4,162.30 (-0.95%) -- even as GDX bucks the tape at $87.78 (+1.20%)
items.summary: Friday's last US close saw bullion ETFs and futures fade despite the weak payrolls print, as the persistently elevated 10-year Treasury yield kept pressure on the metals into the weekend; GLD fell 0.68% to $380.14 and SLV fell 0.51% to $54.74, while COMEX silver (SI=F) dropped 1.23% to $59.98 and gold (GC=F) fell 0.95% to $4,162.30. Miners decoupled again, with GDX gaining 1.20% to $87.78 even as the metal it tracks sold off, consistent with the pattern seen through the week.
items.actionable: This is the base-case backdrop the whole silver/miner sleeve reopens against Monday in Asia -- metals soft, miners resilient -- so there is no fresh signal here to chase or trim ahead of the Asia open; watch whether GDX's outperformance over the metal continues once SGX/HK trading resumes.

items.headline: September payrolls crater to +29,000 (vs ~89k consensus), unemployment hits 4.2% -- stocks rallied into Friday's close (S&P 7,722.72, Nasdaq 27,190.86, VIX 15.31) but didn't pull yields or gold down with them
items.summary: The BLS reported just +29,000 nonfarm payrolls for September versus roughly 84-90k consensus, with unemployment rising to 4.2% (vs 4.1% forecast); August was revised down to +133k. Markets read it as bad-news-is-good-news for Fed policy into Friday's close -- the S&P 500 rose 0.73% to 7,722.72, the Nasdaq gained 1.19% to 27,190.86 and the VIX fell 6.59% to 15.31 -- while fed-funds futures moved toward pricing a hold (not a cut) at the October 27-28 FOMC meeting.
items.actionable: A weak labor print that still can't force a near-term Fed cut (odds remain concentrated on a hold, not easing) means the opportunity-cost drag on the large SGD cash pile isn't going away this month, and it keeps the silver/miner sleeve dependent on real yields rather than rate-cut hopes for its next leg.

items.headline: 10-year Treasury yield holds near a 24-year high above 5.3% on energy-driven inflation fear -- October FOMC odds now split ~83% hold / ~17% hike, essentially 0% cut
items.summary: The 10-year Treasury yield topped 5.34% intraday and the 30-year hit 5.67%, the highest since early 2002, as persistent oil-driven inflation fear keeps the bond market pricing tighter policy risk than the soft labor data alone would suggest. As of October 2, fed-funds futures put a quarter-point hike at roughly 17% and a hold at about 84% for the October 28 decision, with a cut priced at only about 2% -- an unusual setup where inflation risk, not growth risk, is the market's dominant worry.
items.actionable: A 24-year-high real-yield backdrop with the Fed more likely to hike than cut on October 28 is a genuine headwind for gold/silver's carry cost and for SGX REIT refinancing, even as it's a tailwind for DBS/OCBC/UOB net interest margins -- the single most important date to track before Asia opens Monday is still three weeks out.

items.headline: Hang Seng plunges 2.60% to 23,972.29 (steepest drop since March) on first trading day back from National Day -- Tencent $421.20 (-2.27%), Xiaomi $24.24 (-3.96%), SMIC $60.25 (-0.66%) all end the week lower, with Stock Connect still dark until Oct 8
items.summary: Hong Kong stocks suffered their heaviest one-day fall in more than six months on Friday as the market reopened after the National Day holiday into a global bond selloff, with mainland buyers absent (Stock Connect stays suspended until October 8) and weak Macau gaming data adding to the drag. By Friday's close Tencent fell 2.27% to $421.20, Xiaomi dropped 3.96% to $24.24 and SMIC slipped 0.66% to $60.25; the Hang Seng Tech Index fell 2.26% and the Hang Seng China Enterprises Index lost 2.31%.
items.actionable: This selloff happened entirely without mainland liquidity, so the real test for the HK tech sleeve is Monday's pre-open positioning and then October 8 when Stock Connect flow returns -- expect an amplified move (relief or further selling) once mainland participation resumes rather than treating Friday's level as a stable base.

items.headline: Russia hits a major Kyiv bridge for the third straight day; 131 of 157 drones intercepted overnight -- infrastructure campaign escalating into the weekend
items.summary: A Russian drone struck Kyiv's Pivnichnyi Bridge on October 3, damaging the roadway and trolleybus infrastructure and forcing its closure to traffic, two days after four strikes on the capital's Pivdennyi Bridge on Oct 1-2; two people were injured. Ukraine's Air Force said Russia launched 157 attack and decoy drones overnight into Saturday, with air defenses shooting down or neutralizing 131 of them, underscoring a sustained campaign to degrade Kyiv's infrastructure ahead of winter.
items.actionable: A visibly escalating, not de-escalating, war heading into the Monday Asia open supports keeping some gold/silver safe-haven exposure live rather than fading it, though the direct portfolio linkage is more sentiment than fundamentals given no holdings have direct Russia/Ukraine exposure.

items.headline: Moldova summons Russian ambassador after five Russian missiles/drones explode on its territory overnight -- Sandu says "Russia's war is dangerously reaching" the country
items.summary: Three Russian missiles and two drones exploded on Moldovan territory between roughly 7:45-8:00am on October 3 during Russia's latest overnight attack on neighboring Ukraine, with explosions and debris reported across several districts near Anenii Noi, Stefan Voda and Causeni; no casualties were reported. Moldovan President Maia Sandu said Moscow "is putting lives at risk across Europe and must be stopped," and Moldova's government formally summoned Russia's ambassador over the incursions.
items.actionable: A NATO-adjacent country reporting direct Russian weapons impacts for the first time in this cycle is a modest fresh escalation data point for the European tail-risk premium embedded in gold -- worth monitoring for spillover headlines but not yet a reason to add to the safe-haven sleeve on this alone.

items.headline: Bitcoin holds ~$84,800-85,200 through the weekend, trading almost independently of equities -- live level ~$84,772 (+0.33%), total crypto market cap near $2.99tn
items.summary: Bitcoin traded in an $83,898-$85,238 range into Saturday evening and was still near $84,800-85,200 through Sunday, with the broader crypto market cap up 1.1% to roughly $2.99 trillion; analysts noted bitcoin is moving as independently of the US stock market as it has in years, a decoupling that has persisted through the week's Treasury-yield spike. Note crypto trades continuously, so this is a live level rather than a session close, unlike every other asset in this file.
items.actionable: The portfolio has no direct crypto holdings, but bitcoin's decoupling from the equity/yield selloff that is hurting HK tech and bullion is a useful read on risk appetite -- if it holds into Monday's Asia open it argues the yield-driven selloff is idiosyncratic to rate-sensitive assets rather than a broad risk-off event.

items.headline: Oil diverges into the weekend close -- WTI falls 1.90% to $91.11, Brent only -0.06% to $102.25 -- as Hormuz/Houthi tail risk stays live
items.summary: WTI settled Friday at $91.11 (-1.90% on the day) while Brent held up far better at $102.25 (-0.06%), a widening divergence against a backdrop of continued Strait of Hormuz vessel-strike reports and Houthi missile activity toward Saudi Arabia that has kept a geopolitical premium in global (Brent) crude even as the more US-centric WTI benchmark softened on demand concerns.
items.actionable: The Brent/WTI divergence is a signal the oil market is pricing geopolitical supply risk, not demand strength -- relevant to the portfolio mainly as a continued source of the energy-driven inflation fear that is keeping the 10-year yield elevated and pressuring the silver/miner sleeve.

items.headline: Lynas agrees to buy Brazil's Meteoric Resources for ~A$968m, securing the largest ionic-clay rare-earth deposit outside China -- deepens the ex-China supply thesis even as the stock drops on deal dilution
items.summary: Gina Rinehart-backed Lynas Rare Earths signed a binding all-scrip deal worth about A$968 million ($670m) to acquire Meteoric Resources' Caldeira project in Brazil, giving it access to a major new source of the heavy rare earths (dysprosium, terbium) that Lynas is currently the only company outside China to commercially separate at scale. The stock fell on dilution concerns even as the deal strengthens the non-China supply chain that underpins the broader rare-earths watchlist thesis.
items.actionable: This is a structurally bullish deal for the ex-China rare-earth thesis underlying the watchlist even though it's pressuring Lynas shares near-term on deal-dilution mechanics -- a reason to look through the price action rather than read it as a thesis reversal.

items.headline: DBS closes Friday at $77.21 (-0.19%) heading into its October 12 Asia Future Forward Conference with 700+ clients and marquee speakers including PM Lawrence Wong, TikTok's Shou Chew and Broadcom's Hock Tan
items.summary: DBS shares were roughly flat into the weekend at $77.21 (-0.19%) as the bank prepares to host its new flagship DBS Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore on October 12, drawing over 700 corporate and wealth clients with speakers including Singapore PM Lawrence Wong, TikTok CEO Shou Chew, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan, Broadcom President/CEO Hock Tan and Franklin Templeton CEO Jenny Johnson. Separately, DBS arranged a S$79m MSME loan securitisation this week with CapitaLand Investment subscribing the senior notes, part of CapitaLand's ongoing real-estate private-credit strategy.
items.actionable: Nothing here moves the thesis on the SGX bank sleeve directly, but the October 12 conference is a calendar date worth watching for any forward guidance DBS management gives on net interest margins given the current high-yield backdrop that's broadly favorable to the banks.

items.headline: CityDev (C09.SI) craters ~14.8% for the week to S$7.04 -- investors punish the Kwek family's S$5bn China/Japan reinvestment plan announced alongside a S$6bn divestment drive
items.summary: City Developments unveiled a strategic review on September 28 pairing a targeted S$6 billion of divestments over three years with up to S$5 billion earmarked for new investments split 60%-30%-10% across Singapore, China and Japan -- a plan the market read as largely offsetting its own capital-recycling logic rather than returning capital to shareholders. The stock fell 8.1% that day to S$7.59, its worst performance since April 2025 and the worst performer on the Straits Times Index, and continued bleeding through the week to close Friday at roughly S$7.04.
items.actionable: This reads as a company-specific capital-allocation credibility problem -- the market wanted net capital return, not a reinvestment pivot into China/Japan real estate -- rather than a signal on Singapore property broadly, so it argues against treating CityDev's drop as a reason to de-risk the SGX developer/REIT sleeve generally.

items.headline: Silver market on track for a sixth straight annual structural deficit; London free-float liquidity has rebuilt from 2025's crisis lows but remains structurally tight
items.summary: The Silver Institute projects 2026 demand will outrun mine output plus recycling by roughly 46.3 million ounces, extending a run of deficits that began in 2021 and has now drawn down roughly 762 million ounces of above-ground stock; solar, EV and AI-data-center demand continues to grow regardless of price. London's lease-rate crisis has eased materially from October 2025's ~39% spike -- one-month lease rates were back near 0.15% as of this spring -- but the underlying free-float buffer (~28% of vault holdings versus ~17% at the 2025 trough) remains thin relative to demand growth.
items.actionable: This is the slower-moving structural case underneath the levered silver/miner sleeve -- a sixth consecutive deficit year argues the current high-yield-driven pullback is a cyclical headwind on top of a structurally bullish multi-year setup, not a reason to question the core position.

note: 12 items published. This run happens Sunday 2026-10-04 07:02 SGT, before Asia's Monday open, with the last US close Friday 2026-10-02 -- all US/HK/Singapore-market items are framed as that Friday close rather than a live Sunday quote. Three items are dated strictly 2026-10-03 (the Kyiv bridge strike, the Moldova drone/missile incursion) or span into 2026-10-04 (Bitcoin's weekend trading range), satisfying the minimum bar for genuinely fresh 24-48h weekend coverage; a broader Sunday-specific sweep of Singapore and China news turned up only lifestyle/events content and no material new market-moving items beyond what's captured here, so the weekend geopolitics and crypto items carry the freshness load this cycle. The silver structural-deficit and CityDev items are slower-moving/carried-over theses still live from the prior ~5-7 days and are ranked lower accordingly.
